subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What is the highest mountain in the United Kingdom?
questions.explain: Ben Nevis in the Scottish Highlands, at 1,345 m, is the UK's highest peak.

questions.q: Which is the longest river in the United Kingdom?
questions.explain: The River Severn is the UK's longest river at around 354 km, just ahead of the Thames.

questions.q: The United Kingdom is made up of which four nations?
options: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland
England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland
Great Britain, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland
questions.explain: The UK comprises England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the pattern of relief across the UK?
options: Uplands lie mainly in the north and west; lowlands mainly in the south and east
Uplands lie mainly in the south and east; lowlands mainly in the north and west
Uplands are spread evenly across the whole country
Lowlands are found only along the coastline
questions.explain: Higher, older upland areas such as the Scottish Highlands and Pennines dominate the north and west, while flatter lowlands lie in the south and east.

questions.q: Why is population density generally low in the Scottish Highlands?
options: High relief and a harsh upland climate make settlement and farming difficult
The area has the warmest, flattest land in the UK
Government policy bans people from living there
It contains the UK's largest cities and ports
questions.explain: Steep, mountainous terrain and a cold, wet climate limit farming and settlement, keeping the Highlands sparsely populated.

questions.q: Which upland range is often described as the 'backbone of England'?
questions.explain: The Pennines run down the middle of northern England and are commonly called the 'backbone of England'.

questions.q: In which year was the most recent UK census carried out?
questions.explain: The most recent UK census was conducted in 2021 (2022 in Scotland).

questions.q: Approximately what is the total population of the United Kingdom?
questions.explain: The UK's population is around 67 million people according to the 2021 census.

questions.q: Natural increase in a population is calculated as:
questions.explain: Natural increase is the birth rate minus the death rate, excluding the effects of migration.

questions.q: What is the main cause of the UK's ageing population?
options: Rising life expectancy combined with a falling birth rate
High death rates among older people
Large-scale emigration of young adults only
questions.explain: People are living longer while fewer babies are born, so the proportion of older people rises.

questions.q: Which is a likely consequence of the UK's ageing population?
options: Increased pressure on healthcare and pension provision
A sharp fall in demand for medical services
A rapid rise in the number of primary schools needed
A reduction in government spending on care
questions.explain: More elderly people increases demand for healthcare, social care and state pensions.

questions.q: What does the term 'net migration' mean?
options: The number of immigrants minus the number of emigrants
The total number of people entering a country
The number of births minus the number of deaths
The total population of a country
questions.explain: Net migration is immigration minus emigration; a positive figure means more people arrive than leave.

questions.q: In one UK region, there are now more people aged over 65 than people aged under 16. This is clear evidence of:
questions.explain: A greater share of elderly than young people is a defining feature of an ageing population.

questions.q: In one year a country records 700,000 births and 600,000 deaths. What is its natural change?
questions.explain: Natural change = births (700,000) minus deaths (600,000) = an increase of 100,000.

questions.q: Jobs in the tertiary sector of the economy involve:
options: Providing services such as retail, health and education
Extracting raw materials such as farming and mining
Manufacturing and processing goods in factories
questions.explain: The tertiary sector provides services, which now employ the majority of the UK workforce.

questions.q: What does the term 'deindustrialisation' describe in the UK?
options: The decline of manufacturing and the secondary sector
The expansion of coal mining and heavy industry
The movement of people into farming jobs
questions.explain: Deindustrialisation is the fall in manufacturing employment and output that has reshaped the UK economy.

questions.q: Which statement best summarises the UK's 'North-South divide'?
options: Southern England, especially the South East, is generally more economically prosperous than much of the North
Northern England is consistently wealthier than the South
Wealth is spread evenly across all UK regions
questions.explain: The North-South divide describes generally higher incomes and economic activity in the South East compared with parts of the North.

questions.q: A former industrial town sees its steel factory close, while new call centres, offices and shops open. This change best illustrates:
options: A shift from the secondary to the tertiary sector
A shift from tertiary to secondary employment
questions.explain: Loss of manufacturing (secondary) jobs and growth of service (tertiary) jobs reflects the UK's changing employment structure.

questions.q: The UK is one of five permanent members of which international body?
questions.explain: The UK is one of the five permanent members of the UN Security Council, alongside the USA, Russia, China and France.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of the UK's cultural influence around the world?
options: The global reach of the BBC and the English language
Its permanent seat on the UN Security Council
Its membership of NATO's military alliance
Its provision of overseas development aid
questions.explain: UK media exports such as the BBC, along with the worldwide use of English, spread British culture globally.

questions.q: A UK-based transnational corporation (TNC) opens factories and offices in several other countries. This best demonstrates the UK's:
options: Economic role in the wider world
questions.explain: UK TNCs operating overseas show the country's economic influence and links in the global economy.

specSource: OCR GCSE (9–1) Geography (B) (J384) specification; UK in the 21st Century
